chunks: "Because the capacitor is only useful if it can deliver current faster than the chip changes its demand, and everything between the capacitor and the pin is inductance.
Every millimetre of trace or via adds roughly half a nanohenry to a nanohenry, and the voltage across that inductance is L times di/dt.
A chip stepping 50 milliamps per nanosecond through 1 nanohenry takes 50 millivolts of droop right there, no matter how big the capacitor is.
Put the capacitor 20 millimetres away and that's 10 to 20 nanohenries and a volt of droop.

That inductance also resonates against the chip's own capacitance, which drops the anti-resonance into the chip's active band, and the long loop, from capacitor to pin and back through the ground, radiates and picks up noise.
And the part of the loop you can't remove, the package pin and bond wire, already uses up some of the budget, which is why the closest you can get is what counts.
It's inductance rather than delay that matters.
The signal delay over 20 millimetres is only about 130 picoseconds, which is short compared to a nanosecond edge, but the inductance is already ruinous.
So the rule isn't about waves, it's about L di/dt."
